prompt: A page has a title at the top of a section. Which element fits its meaning?
optionB: A heading element
optionC: A list item, for the indentation
optionD: A quote element, which stands out
correctAnswerText: A heading element
explanation: A heading element says that the text titles what follows, which is what the content is. The other three would be chosen for how they look rather than for what they mean.

prompt: A page shows three product names, one after another, with no ordering between them. Which element fits?
optionB: An ordered list, since they appear in an order on screen
optionC: A table with one column
optionD: An unordered list
correctAnswerText: An unordered list
explanation: A group of related items with no meaningful order is exactly what an unordered list expresses. Appearing one after another on screen is not the same as being ordered.

prompt: A page reproduces a sentence taken from another source. Which element fits?
optionB: A paragraph in italics
optionC: A list item, which indents it
optionD: A heading, to set it apart
correctAnswerText: A quotation element
explanation: The content is a quotation, and one element says so. Italics and indentation are how quotations often look, which is a consequence rather than the meaning.

prompt: A developer uses a heading element because it makes the text large. What is wrong with that?
optionA: Nothing; the text is the right size
optionB: Headings should never be used
optionC: The element says the text is a heading, which will be untrue and will mislead anything reading the structure
optionD: The text will be the wrong size on some screens
correctAnswerText: The element says the text is a heading, which will be untrue and will mislead anything reading the structure
explanation: Choosing an element for its appearance puts a false claim into the document. Size can be set directly without changing what the markup says the content is.

prompt: Two developers produce pages that look identical. One used headings for its section titles and the other used styled paragraphs. What differs?
optionB: What the document says its structure is, which anything other than a sighted reader depends on
optionC: The file size
optionD: How quickly each page loads
correctAnswerText: What the document says its structure is, which anything other than a sighted reader depends on
explanation: Appearance is the same and meaning is not. A reader navigating by structure, or a tool building an outline, sees sections in one page and undifferentiated text in the other.

prompt: Which fragment is written correctly?
optionB: Hello
optionC: Hello
optionD: Hello
correctAnswerText: Hello
explanation: An element that holds content opens and closes once around it. Repeating the opening tag opens a second element, and a second closing tag closes something that is not open.

prompt: An image is being placed on a page. Which fragment is written correctly?
optionC: cat.png
explanation: An image element holds no content, so it takes no closing tag and its source is supplied as an attribute. Giving it content or a closing tag treats it like an element that wraps something.

prompt: Which fragment closes its tags in the right order?
optionB: text
optionC: text
optionD: text
correctAnswerText: text
explanation: Elements close in the reverse of the order they open, so the inner one closes first. Crossing them leaves each element half inside the other, which nothing can represent.

prompt: A paragraph element is opened and never closed, and the rest of the page follows. What happens to that later content?
optionB: It may be absorbed into the unclosed element, so it is treated as part of the paragraph
optionC: The page refuses to render
optionD: It renders exactly as though the tag had been closed
correctAnswerText: It may be absorbed into the unclosed element, so it is treated as part of the paragraph
explanation: An element that is never closed continues, so what follows falls inside it. The page still renders, which is why the fault shows up as misplaced content rather than as an error.

prompt: In Help, which part is an attribute?
optionB: Help
optionD: href="/help"
correctAnswerText: href="/help"
explanation: The attribute is href="/help", a name-and-value pair inside the opening tag. The letter at the front is the element name and the word between the tags is the content.

prompt: In , what does the alt attribute supply?
optionA: Text to use in place of the image
optionB: The file the image comes from
optionC: The name of the element
optionD: The width of the image
correctAnswerText: Text to use in place of the image
explanation: Each attribute supplies one thing, and this one supplies the alternative text. The file is supplied by a different attribute in the same tag.

prompt: Where do attributes belong?
optionB: In either tag
optionC: In the opening tag
optionD: Between the opening and closing tags, with the content
correctAnswerText: In the opening tag
explanation: Attributes configure the element and are written where it opens. A closing tag carries the element name and nothing else.

prompt: A tag reads Help, with no quotation marks around the value. Is the value part of the attribute or content?
optionA: Content, because it is not quoted
optionB: Part of the attribute; it sits inside the opening tag whether or not it is quoted
optionC: Neither; the tag is invalid and is ignored
optionD: Part of the element name
correctAnswerText: Part of the attribute; it sits inside the opening tag whether or not it is quoted
explanation: What decides is position rather than punctuation: anything inside the opening tag after the element name is an attribute. Quoting is good practice and its absence does not move the value out of the tag.

prompt: Which fragment nests correctly?
optionB: • One
optionC: • One
optionD: • One
correctAnswerText: • One
explanation: A list contains list items and an item may contain anything inline. Placing an emphasis element directly inside the list, or crossing the closing tags, breaks the containment.

prompt:
A fragment reads

Some bold

text. What is wrong, and what will happen?
optionA: The two elements overlap rather than nest, and the browser will guess at a structure
optionB: Nothing; the tags are all present
optionC: The strong element is missing a closing tag
optionD: The paragraph is missing an opening tag
correctAnswerText: The two elements overlap rather than nest, and the browser will guess at a structure
explanation: Every tag is present and they cross, which is what no tree can represent. Browsers recover by inventing a structure, and different ones may invent different structures.

prompt: Text is to be emphasised because it is genuinely important. Two elements render it in bold. Which fits?
optionA: The one that means the text should be bold
optionB: Either; they render the same
optionC: The one that means the text is important
optionD: A generic container with bold styling
correctAnswerText: The one that means the text is important
explanation: Both look the same and only one says why the text is different. That claim is what anything reading the structure rather than the pixels acts on.

prompt: A page has a block of navigation links. A generic container and a navigation element both produce the same appearance. Which fits, and why does it matter?
optionA: The generic container, because it is more flexible
optionB: The navigation element, because it lets a reader jump to or skip the navigation
optionC: Either; the appearance is what users see
optionD: The generic container, because it is shorter to type
correctAnswerText: The navigation element, because it lets a reader jump to or skip the navigation
explanation: A specific element exists for this content and carries information a generic one does not. Flexibility and brevity are real considerations and neither restores what the meaning would have supplied.

prompt:
A fragment reads

Hello world

, with five spaces between the words. What appears on the page?
optionB: Helloworld, with no space
optionC: The text with the tags shown
optionD: Hello world, with a single space
correctAnswerText: Hello world, with a single space
explanation: Runs of whitespace collapse to one space when rendered. Tags are instructions rather than content and are not displayed.

prompt: A fragment has a paragraph whose text is written across three lines in the file, with no other markup. How does it appear?
optionA: As one continuous line of text, wrapped to fit the width
optionB: As three separate lines, as written
optionC: As three separate paragraphs
optionD: With the line breaks shown as blank lines
correctAnswerText: As one continuous line of text, wrapped to fit the width
explanation: A newline in the source is whitespace and collapses like any other. Breaking lines on the page requires markup that says so.

prompt: A developer formats their markup neatly across several lines and the rendered spacing between two words changes. The markup is valid and the elements are unchanged. What happened?
optionB: The browser reformatted the text
optionC: A newline was introduced where the two words previously touched, and it renders as a space
optionD: Nothing changed; the difference is imagined
correctAnswerText: A newline was introduced where the two words previously touched, and it renders as a space
explanation: Collapsing whitespace turns a newline into one space, so a line break inserted between two words adds a space that was not there. Reformatting markup is usually safe and is not always so.

prompt: A list fragment contains three list items and one line of text placed directly inside the list itself. How many list items does it have?
optionB: Three
optionC: One
optionD: Three, plus a fourth once the text is wrapped
correctAnswerText: Three
explanation: Only content inside a list item counts as an item. The stray text is inside the list and inside no item, which is why it is not counted and is also not valid.

prompt: A table has a header row of 3 cells and 4 further rows of 3 cells each. How many cells does it contain in total?
explanation: Every row contributes its cells, header rows included, so five rows of three give fifteen. Omitting the header row is the commonest miscount.

prompt: A table is meant to have 4 columns. One row contains 3 cells and the rest contain 4. The markup is otherwise valid and the page renders. What is the effect?
optionA: That row is short by a cell, so its remaining cells may not line up with the columns above
optionB: The table refuses to render
optionC: The missing cell is created automatically and left blank
optionD: The whole table is reduced to three columns
correctAnswerText: That row is short by a cell, so its remaining cells may not line up with the columns above
explanation: A row supplies exactly the cells it contains, and nothing fills a gap. The table still renders, which is why the fault appears as misaligned data rather than as an error.

prompt: A site has /index.html and /about.html. A link in index.html reads href="about.html". Which file does it reach?
optionB: A file called about.html inside a folder called about
optionC: /about.html
optionD: Nothing; the path is incomplete
correctAnswerText: /about.html
explanation: A path with no leading slash is resolved beside the page containing it, and both files sit at the top level. Nothing about it is incomplete.

prompt: The folder tree is: index.html at the top level, and a guides folder containing setup.html. A link written inside setup.html begins with a slash: href="/index.html". What does the leading slash change?
optionA: Nothing; a leading slash is optional
optionB: It resolves from the top of the site rather than from the folder the page is in
optionC: It resolves from the folder the page is in, as usual
optionD: It makes the link point outside the site
correctAnswerText: It resolves from the top of the site rather than from the folder the page is in
explanation: A leading slash starts the path at the root, so the same text means the same file wherever the page sits. Without it the link would be looked for inside the guides folder.

prompt: A site has /guides/setup.html and /images/logo.png. A link in setup.html reads href="../images/logo.png" and works. The same link is copied into /index.html and breaks. Neither file was moved. Why?
optionB: A leading slash is missing from both links
optionC: index.html cannot reach the images folder
optionD: The parent step goes up one level from wherever the page is, and from the top level there is nowhere to go up to
correctAnswerText: The parent step goes up one level from wherever the page is, and from the top level there is nowhere to go up to
explanation: A relative path is measured from the page containing it, so the same text means different things in different places. From the top level the parent step overshoots the site entirely.

prompt: A form contains a text input with no name attribute. Is its value submitted?
optionA: No; a control without a name has nothing to submit its value under
optionB: Yes; the value is submitted under its label
optionC: Yes; the value is submitted without a name
optionD: No; the form refuses to submit at all
correctAnswerText: No; a control without a name has nothing to submit its value under
explanation: The name is what the value is sent as, so a control without one is silently omitted. The form submits normally, which is what makes the omission hard to spot.

prompt: A form contains a disabled text input with a name and a value. Is its value submitted?
optionA: Yes; it has a name and a value
optionB: Yes; disabling only prevents editing
optionC: No; a disabled control is excluded from the submission
optionD: No; and the form refuses to submit
correctAnswerText: No; a disabled control is excluded from the submission
explanation: Disabling removes the control from the submission as well as from interaction. That is different from making it read-only, which prevents editing and still submits.

prompt: A form has a checkbox that the user leaves unchecked. The server receives no value for it and treats the field as missing rather than false. The checkbox has a name and the form submits correctly. What is happening?
optionB: An unchecked box submits nothing at all, so absence is the only signal that it was unchecked
optionC: The checkbox has no name
optionD: The form is submitting before the box is read
correctAnswerText: An unchecked box submits nothing at all, so absence is the only signal that it was unchecked
explanation: A checkbox submits its value only when checked, so unchecked and absent are indistinguishable on the server. The stem rules out the name and the submission, which leaves the behaviour itself.

prompt: An image is a company logo appearing in the page header. What alternative text fits?
optionB: A rectangular blue image with white lettering
optionC: Image
optionD: The company name
correctAnswerText: The company name
explanation: Alternative text conveys what the image conveys, which here is the company's identity. A filename and a description of the appearance both leave the reader without the information the image carried.

prompt: An image is a chart showing sales rising over four quarters. What alternative text fits?
optionA: A statement of what the chart shows, such as that sales rose across the four quarters
optionB: chart.png
optionC: A line chart with four points
optionD: Chart
correctAnswerText: A statement of what the chart shows, such as that sales rose across the four quarters
explanation: The image carries a finding, so the alternative text has to carry that finding. Describing the shape of the chart gives the reader the picture without the point.

prompt: An image is a decorative flourish beside a heading and conveys nothing a reader needs. Every option below is a well-formed value. What alternative text fits?
optionB: The word "decoration"
optionC: Empty text, so that the image is passed over
optionD: The filename
correctAnswerText: Empty text, so that the image is passed over
explanation: An image carrying no information should not interrupt a reader, and empty alternative text is how that is expressed. Describing it, or announcing that it is decorative, makes the reader stop for something that does not matter.

prompt:
A fragment reads:

One two

Three

. What is the parent of the em element?
optionB: The first paragraph
optionC: The second paragraph
optionD: The text "One"
correctAnswerText: The first paragraph
explanation: A parent is the element that directly contains another, and the em sits inside The first paragraph. The div is its grandparent rather than its parent.

prompt: In the same fragment, someone says the em element and the second paragraph are siblings. Both are contained within the div at some depth. Are they?
optionA: Yes; both are inside the div
optionB: Yes; they are at the same visual level
optionC: No; the em element has no siblings at all
optionD: No; siblings share the same direct parent, and these have different ones
correctAnswerText: No; siblings share the same direct parent, and these have different ones
explanation: Being inside the same ancestor is not the same as sharing a parent, which is what makes the claim tempting. The em element does have a sibling — the text beside it in the first paragraph.

prompt: A page shows its whole second half in bold. The markup contains an opening emphasis tag halfway down. Which line is at fault?
optionA: The line with the opening emphasis tag, which is never closed
optionB: The first line of the bold text
optionC: The last line of the page
optionD: The stylesheet, which must set bold
correctAnswerText: The line with the opening emphasis tag, which is never closed
explanation: The symptom starts where the element opens and continues because nothing closes it. The lines that appear bold are affected rather than responsible.

prompt: A page shows its navigation links inside the first article rather than above it. The stylesheet is unchanged and correct, and the navigation markup itself is well formed. Which kind of fault is it?
optionA: A styling fault in the navigation
optionB: A fault in the navigation markup
optionC: A structural one: something before the navigation was left unclosed, so it was absorbed
optionD: A fault in the article markup, which is too wide
correctAnswerText: A structural one: something before the navigation was left unclosed, so it was absorbed
explanation: Content appearing in the wrong place with correct styling and correct local markup points at an unclosed element earlier in the document. The cause sits before the symptom, which is what makes it awkward to find.

prompt: A form shows the word "Email" beside a text box, written as plain text with no association between them. What can a screen reader user not do?
optionB: Know what the box is for when they reach it
optionC: Type into the box
optionD: Submit the form
correctAnswerText: Know what the box is for when they reach it
explanation: The text is visible and unconnected, so a reader moving to the control is told nothing about it. Everything else on the page continues to work, which is why the fault is invisible on screen.

prompt: A page uses a top-level heading, then jumps to a third-level heading for its next section. The page looks correct and the headings are real heading elements. What is lost?
optionB: The headings will not be announced at all
optionC: The second-level heading is created automatically
optionD: The outline implies a missing level, so a reader navigating by structure cannot tell how the sections relate
correctAnswerText: The outline implies a missing level, so a reader navigating by structure cannot tell how the sections relate
explanation: Heading levels describe nesting, and skipping one describes a nesting that does not exist. Everything is announced and the relationships between the sections are wrong.

prompt: A developer fixes an accessibility complaint by increasing the font size and the contrast. The complaint was that a form control had no label. Has the complaint been addressed?
optionA: No; the fix is visual and the fault is structural, so a reader who cannot see it is no better off
optionB: Yes; the page is now easier to read
optionC: Yes, provided the contrast is sufficient
optionD: No; the font size should have been left alone
correctAnswerText: No; the fix is visual and the fault is structural, so a reader who cannot see it is no better off
explanation: The change is a genuine improvement for some readers and touches nothing the complaint was about. Matching the kind of fix to the kind of fault is what makes accessibility work rather than gesture.

prompt: Two pages look identical. One uses heading elements and lists; the other uses styled generic containers throughout. What can a reader do on one and not the other?
optionA: Read the text, which only the first page allows
optionB: See the page, which only the first page allows
optionC: Navigate by structure — jump between sections, or move through a list — which only the marked-up page supports
optionD: Nothing differs; both pages carry the same information
correctAnswerText: Navigate by structure — jump between sections, or move through a list — which only the marked-up page supports
explanation: Both pages present the same words and only one says how they are organised. Structure is what navigation is built on, so its absence removes a way of moving through the page rather than the content.

prompt: Adding correct structure to a page costs a little time and changes nothing visible. Why is it worth doing?
optionA: Because it makes the page load faster
optionB: Because the structure is what every non-visual route through the page depends on, and nothing else supplies it
optionC: Because it makes the page look better
optionD: It is not worth doing if nothing changes visually
correctAnswerText: Because the structure is what every non-visual route through the page depends on, and nothing else supplies it
explanation: Nothing changing visually is exactly the point: the benefit accrues to readers who are not using the visual presentation at all. Judging the change by what it does to the picture measures the wrong thing.

prompt: A page is correct until its third section, after which everything is indented and misplaced. The third section's own markup is well formed. Where is the fault?
optionA: In the third section, where the symptom begins
optionB: In the last section, which is most affected
optionC: In the stylesheet, which indents the content
optionD: In an element opened before the third section and never closed
correctAnswerText: In an element opened before the third section and never closed
explanation: An unclosed element absorbs everything after it, so the symptom starts where the effect begins and the cause sits earlier. The section where trouble first appears is the one being affected.

prompt: Why is an unclosed tag harder to locate than a misspelled element name?
optionA: Its effect appears at a distance from its cause, and everything between them looks correct
optionB: Because browsers hide unclosed tags
optionC: Because a misspelled name is always reported as an error
optionD: It is not harder; both are equally visible
correctAnswerText: Its effect appears at a distance from its cause, and everything between them looks correct
explanation: The symptom of an unclosed tag is displaced from the line responsible, so reading around the symptom finds nothing wrong. A misspelling affects the element it appears on.

prompt: A page has one unclosed element near the top and renders as one enormous nested block. How many faults should be looked for?
optionB: At least two, since one tag cannot affect so much
optionC: One; a single unclosed element can misplace everything after it
optionD: None; the browser recovers automatically
correctAnswerText: One; a single unclosed element can misplace everything after it
explanation: The scale of a symptom says nothing about the number of causes, and containment cascades through everything that follows. Browsers do recover, and the structure they invent is what produces the symptom.

prompt: A developer proposes fixing misplaced content by adding closing tags at the end of the document. What is wrong with that?
optionA: Nothing; the tags are now balanced
optionB: It closes the elements in the wrong place, so the content is still inside them
optionC: Closing tags may not appear at the end of a document
optionD: It would make the page refuse to render
correctAnswerText: It closes the elements in the wrong place, so the content is still inside them
explanation: Balance is not the requirement; the element has to close where its content ends. Closing everything at the bottom produces a well-formed document with exactly the wrong structure.

prompt: Browsers recover from unclosed tags rather than refusing to render. What does that buy, and what does it cost?
optionA: It buys nothing; strictness would be better
optionB: It costs nothing; recovery is always correct
optionC: It buys speed, since no checking is needed
optionD: It keeps imperfect pages usable, and it lets a structural fault reach users without anything reporting it
correctAnswerText: It keeps imperfect pages usable, and it lets a structural fault reach users without anything reporting it
explanation: Recovery is why a small mistake does not take a page down, and it is also why the mistake is never announced. Different browsers may recover differently, so the same page can render differently for different people.

prompt: Two fragments render identically: one uses a heading element, the other a paragraph styled to match. Both look the same in every browser tested. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; they look alike and say different things about what the content is
optionB: Yes; identical rendering is what equivalence means
optionC: No; they will render differently on some browsers
optionD: Yes, provided the styling is applied everywhere
correctAnswerText: No; they look alike and say different things about what the content is
explanation: Equivalence in markup covers structure and meaning as well as appearance. Identical rendering is what makes the difference invisible rather than absent.

prompt: Two fragments differ only in how their whitespace is laid out across lines, with no whitespace inserted between words. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; the layout of the source affects the page
optionB: No; different line lengths render differently
optionC: Yes; whitespace between tags collapses and carries no meaning
optionD: Yes, but only if both are on one line
correctAnswerText: Yes; whitespace between tags collapses and carries no meaning
explanation: Formatting the source is one of the few changes that genuinely preserves both structure and appearance. The exception is whitespace between words, which the stem excludes.

prompt: Two fragments produce the same page: one wraps its content in three nested containers and one in a single container. Are they equivalent?
optionB: In appearance and in meaning yes; they differ in the tree, which styling and scripts may depend on
optionC: No; the extra containers change the meaning
optionD: No; extra containers always change the appearance
correctAnswerText: In appearance and in meaning yes; they differ in the tree, which styling and scripts may depend on
explanation: Containers carry no meaning of their own, so the document says the same thing either way. The shape of the tree is still real, and anything selecting by relationship can tell the two apart.

prompt: What does it take to say two fragments are truly equivalent?
optionB: That they contain the same text
optionC: That they use the same number of elements
optionD: That they agree in structure and meaning as well as in appearance
correctAnswerText: That they agree in structure and meaning as well as in appearance
explanation: Appearance is one of three things a fragment carries, and the other two are what markup exists to express. Two fragments can share their text and their picture while describing entirely different documents.
